Part F · Chapter F2

AI on a robot

Sense, decide, act, on a small computer with a camera.

A robot has a deadline: SharkCam must see a shark, decide and turn its camera before the shark moves on. This chapter adds up the stage times of that loop, then works out memory from the number of weights and frames per second from the multiply-adds per frame. It rounds the weights of a digit-reading network to 8, 4 and 2 bits and measures the cost on 10,000 test digits.

You will need: the digit reader and its parameter counts from C2, the KV cache of D5 for one remark about language models, and the rare classes of A4 for the last exercise. The size of GPT-2 comes from D2 and D5.

Sense, decide, act

Guess first. SharkCam's camera makes 30 pictures a second, so one picture takes 33 milliseconds (ms). The model needs 160 ms for a picture, and the camera then needs 60 ms to turn. Counting from the start of the picture, how old is its information when the turn ends: about 30 ms, about 100 ms or about 250 ms?

A robot repeats a loop: a sensor reads the world (sense), a program chooses a command (decide) and a motor acts (act). SharkCam's loop has four stages: camera, model (the network that looks for sharks), decision and motor. Its latency L is the sum of their times, the age of the information in a command when the motor finishes its turn. Here the program does not predict the shark's motion, so the camera points where the shark was, and the largest angle between that direction and the shark is the pointing error. The time the loop may take follows from the allowed error and the shark's speed and distance, so the model does not set it.

  1. Press Step four times to follow one frame through the stages. The bar below lays the stage times end to end, to scale, up to L = 257 ms.
  2. The last count, a pointing error of 9.8 degrees, is coral because it is above the 5 allowed. Choose MobileNetV2, a smaller network, and the count turns teal.

0latency L: light in to motor moving
0update period T
0worst age of a command, L + T
0pointing error behind the shark

In this example ResNet-18 gives a 257 ms loop and a 9.8 degree error (5 allowed) for a made-up shark crossing at 1 m/s from 3 m, and MobileNetV2 gives 124 ms and 4.7 degrees.

How it works

At the figure's start (ResNet-18 with 8-bit weights on a Raspberry Pi 4) the stages take 36.8 ms (camera: 33.3 for the picture, 3.5 to read it), 159.2 ms (model, estimated), 1 ms (decision) and 60 ms (motor), the last two assumed. Their sum is L = 36.8 + 159.2 + 1 + 60 = 257 ms. With one frame at a time, the robot takes the next picture after the motor finishes, so the update period T, the time between two commands, is also 257 ms. A command is up to L + T = 514 ms old when the next one arrives. In the middle of its pass a shark crossing the view at distance d and speed v sweeps ω = v/d radians per second (here 1/3 radian = 19.1 degrees per second), so at worst the camera is behind by about ω(L + T).

19.1ω = v/d, degrees per second (1 m/s, 3 m)×0.514L + T, seconds=9.8pointing error, degrees
  1. Press Play the pass: the gap between the teal line and the coral dashed line is the pointing error, at most 9.8 degrees at the start settings.

Common belief. If the model runs at 30 frames per second, the robot reacts in 33 ms.

Why it fails. Frames per second, 1/T, says how often a command arrives, while latency says how old it is, so the rate alone does not give the reaction time.

Better account. Compare L + T with the budget, the longest sum that keeps the error within the allowed angle: 5 degrees divided by 19.1 degrees per second is 262 ms.

Quick quiz

In the first figure, tick "pipelined", which lets the camera take the next picture while the model works. T falls from 257 to 159 ms. Does L fall too?

No. A frame still goes through the four stages in order. So L, the time from the start of the picture to the end of the turn, stays 257 ms, and only T changes.

The shark swims twice as fast. How does the error change, and how must L + T change to keep it the same?

The error doubles, because ω = v/d doubles. To keep the error the same, L + T must halve.

Go deeper stage times, symbols, second case, Python about 5 min

The four stages

The four boxes of the first figure are the stages, and the bar below them shows the times to scale. The camera stage is the frame interval (33 ms at 30 frames per second) plus 3.5 ms to read and process the picture. The 3.5 ms is the figure the PyTorch tutorial gives for reading and processing the data. Taking the whole frame interval as the camera's time means that the age of the information is counted from the start of the picture. The model stage comes from the calculator of the next section (159.2 ms for ResNet-18 in 8 bits on a Pi 4). The decision is a few lines of code, which we assume takes 1 ms. A small hobby servo is assumed to need 60 ms for a short turn. The camera interval, the decision and the motor time are assumed values, and the shark's speed and distance are made up for the story. The sum is the latency L, the age of the information in the command when the motor has finished its turn.

Pipelining

With "pipelined" switched on, the camera no longer waits for the model, so in the figure the robot gets a new command after 159 ms instead of 257 ms. The latency stays at 257 ms. Pipelining raises the rate of updates and leaves the age of an update unchanged. For a shark that keeps moving, both matter: the command is L old when it arrives, and the next one is T later.

What the lag costs

The second figure shows the cost. The camera points where the shark was at the time of the last frame it used, which is between L and L + T ago. The shark moves on, and the gap between the dashed coral line to the shark and the teal line of the aim is the pointing error. The error grows with the shark's speed and shrinks as the shark swims farther away. The wedge is a 60-degree field of view. The pass starts with the camera on target, and the animation is slowed when the pass would be too quick to watch.

Symbols

0camera, ms+0model, ms+0decision, ms+0motor, ms=0latency L, ms→0L + T, ms (T = 0)×0degrees per second=0pointing error, degrees

\[ L = t_{\text{cam}} + t_{\text{model}} + t_{\text{dec}} + t_{\text{motor}} \]

\[ \theta_{\text{err}} \approx \omega\,(L + T) \qquad \omega = \frac{v}{d} \qquad L + T \le \frac{\theta_{\text{allowed}}}{\omega} \]

  • \(t_{\text{cam}}\), \(t_{\text{model}}\), \(t_{\text{dec}}\) and \(t_{\text{motor}}\) are the times of the four stages. \(L\) is their sum, the latency. \(T\) is the update period: \(L\) when the robot finishes a frame before it takes the next, and the larger of the camera interval and the model time when it is pipelined.
  • \(v\) is the shark's speed across the view in m/s and \(d\) its distance in m. \(\omega\) is the angle it sweeps per second (in radians; the figure shows degrees). The formula is for the middle of the pass, where the angle changes fastest, and it assumes small turns.
  • The last relation is the budget. The budget line on the bar is the longest \(L+T\) that keeps the error within the allowed angle. For 5 degrees at 19.1 degrees per second it is 262 ms.

A second case

MobileNetV2 in 8 bits needs 26 ms in the model. The loop takes 124 ms, the update period is 124 ms when frames are taken one at a time, and the worst command age is 248 ms. That is within the 262 ms budget, with an error of 4.7 degrees. In pipelined mode the period falls to the camera's 33 ms and the error to 3.0 degrees. In this example the smaller model changes the result from missing the allowed error to meeting it. The decision and the motor cost the same in both cases.

My robot

Bridge to my robot. I have built a small robot that ran a vision model on a Raspberry Pi. The questions of this chapter are the ones such a build raises. How large a model fits in the memory? How many frames per second does it give? What does the delay from camera to motor do to how the robot behaves?

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Put a timestamp before and after the stages in the robot's code, and print the stage times. The stage you expect to be slow is not always the slow one. Fix the biggest bar first. Repeat the measurement on the robot, not on a laptop.

In Python

import numpy as np

stages = {"camera": 36.8, "model": 159.3, "decision": 1.0, "motor": 60.0}   # milliseconds
L = sum(stages.values())
v, d = 1.0, 3.0                                   # shark speed in m/s, distance in m
omega = np.degrees(v / d)                         # degrees per second, at the middle of the pass

for name, T in [("one frame at a time", L), ("pipelined", max(33.3, stages["model"]))]:
    lag = L + T                                   # age of the information plus the wait for the next update
    print(f"{name}: latency {L:.0f} ms, new command after {T:.0f} ms, "
          f"pointing error {omega * lag / 1000:.1f} degrees")
one frame at a time: latency 257 ms, new command after 257 ms, pointing error 9.8 degrees
pipelined: latency 257 ms, new command after 159 ms, pointing error 8.0 degrees

Frames per second and memory

Guess first. ResNet-18 is a network that classifies images. For one camera frame it needs about 1.8 billion multiply-adds (a multiply-add is one multiplication and one addition). A Raspberry Pi 4 reached about 11 billion a second on another network, MobileNetV2, with 8-bit integer weights; assume the same here. How many frames per second does the Pi manage: about 6, about 60 or about 600?

Two sums estimate whether a model can run on a robot. The memory sum multiplies the number of weights N by the bytes per weight, b/8, where b is the number of bits per weight. A model can fit only if this memory M is no more than the computer's memory, and a running program needs memory for more than the weights. The time sum divides the multiply-adds O for one frame by the multiply-adds per second R that the computer reaches. This gives the time t the model takes per frame, and so the frames per second f = 1/t. For 16 and 32 bits the figure assumes a speed 2.5 times lower than for 8 bits.

  1. The ringed dot is ResNet-18 at 8 bits on the Pi 4. Its weights take 11.7 MB, far to the left of the dashed coral line (the Pi's 4 GB), and it is estimated at 6.28 frames per second, below the dashed sand line (10 per second, an assumed need).
  2. Choose MobileNetV2, a smaller network, and the dot moves up to 37.9 frames per second. Choose the 70B model (70 billion weights) and 4 bits: its weights still need 35.0 GB, to the right of the coral line.
0memory for the weights,
0time for one frame
0frames (or tokens) per second,
0billion multiply-adds per second at this precision

On a Pi 4, ResNet-18 in 8 bits needs 11.7 MB of weights and is estimated at about 6 frames per second, MobileNetV2 at about 38, and the 70-billion-parameter model needs 35 GB even at 4 bits, against the 4 GB of the Pi 4.

How it works

Take ResNet-18 in 8 bits on the Pi 4. It has N = 11,689,512 parameters, which the figure calls weights, and at b = 8 bits a weight takes 1 byte, so M = 11.7 MB. The speed R comes from one published measurement: the PyTorch tutorial reports 26.4 ms for MobileNetV2 in 8 bits on a Pi 4. That network needs 300.8 million multiply-adds, so R = 300.8 million/0.0264 s = 11.39 billion per second. We use that speed for ResNet-18 too, an assumption, because the networks may use the processor differently. Then its O = 1.814 billion multiply-adds take t = 1.814/11.39 = 0.159 s, so f = 1/t = 6.3 frames per second.

11,689,512weights, N×1byte per weight (8 bits ÷ 8)=11.7 MBmemory M | 1.814 billionmultiply-adds, O÷11.39 billionper second, R=0.159 stime t→6.3per second, 1/t

Common belief. A model with fewer parameters is a faster model.

Why it fails. Parameters set the memory, and the multiply-adds set the time. A convolutional network reuses a weight at all positions of the picture, so a network with few parameters and a large picture can still need many multiply-adds. The digit reader does about 32 multiply-adds per parameter and ResNet-18 about 155.

Better account. Count both numbers, because memory follows the parameters and time follows the multiply-adds divided by the speed you measure.

Quick quiz

A model has 25 million weights stored in 16 bits. How much memory do they need?

\(25\times10^6 \times 16/8 = 50\) million bytes, or 50 MB.

A model does 600 million multiply-adds per frame on a computer that reaches 12 billion per second. How many frames per second, and what if the speed halves?

\(12\times10^9 / (600\times10^6) = 20\) frames per second, or 50 ms per frame. At half the speed the time doubles to 100 ms and the rate halves to 10 per second.

Go deeper speed sources, memory traffic, symbols, Python about 5 min

Terms

A profiler may count the multiplication and the addition of a multiply-add separately and report twice the number. The effective speed is the number of multiply-adds per second that a program reaches, which is usually well below the peak of a spec sheet.

Reading the plot

Choose a model and a number of bits. The dot of the chosen model is ringed. Its position on the left to right axis is the memory of its weights. The dashed coral line is the computer's memory, and any dot to its right does not fit. Its position on the bottom to top axis is the frames per second. The dashed sand line is the rate the robot needs, and any dot below it is too slow. Lower the bits and all the dots move left. From 32 or 16 bits to 8 they also move up, by the speed-up factor you set.

What the calculator assumes

For 8 bits and fewer the calculator uses the 8-bit speed, so 4-bit weights get no speed-up. The assumed reason is that these processors have no 4-bit multiply. Software can still gain from reading fewer bytes.

Symbols

0weights, N×0bits ÷ 8 = bytes per weight=0memory M | 0multiply-adds, O÷0billion per second, R=0time t→0per second, 1/t

\[ M = N\cdot\frac{b}{8} \ \text{bytes} \qquad t = \frac{O}{R_b} \qquad f = \frac{1}{t} \]

\[ R_b = R_8 \ \text{ for } b \le 8 \qquad R_b = R_8 / s_8 \ \text{ for } b > 8 \]

  • \(N\) is the number of weights (the parameters of A1) and \(b\) the bits per weight, so \(b/8\) is the bytes per weight. \(M\) is the memory for the weights alone.
  • \(O\) is the multiply-adds for one frame (one token for a language model). \(R_b\) is the effective speed in multiply-adds per second when the weights have \(b\) bits. \(t\) is the time per frame and \(f\) the frames per second.
  • \(R_8\) is the speed for 8-bit weights. \(s_8\) is how many times slower arithmetic with more than 8 bits is; the figure uses it for 16 and 32 bits. The page assumes 2.5. The LiteRT documentation lists 2 to 3 times for dynamic range quantisation and more than 3 times for full integer quantisation. The actual value depends on the chip.

Where the speeds come from

The speed of a computer in multiply-adds per second is not on its box, and the peak in the spec sheet is not what a program reaches. The page uses one measurement. The PyTorch tutorial for the Raspberry Pi runs MobileNetV2, quantised to 8 bits, on a Pi 4 with 4 GB. It reports 26.4 ms per frame in the model and 29.7 ms in all, about 33.7 frames per second. MobileNetV2 needs 300.8 million multiply-adds (counted for this chapter from the network's definition). Dividing gives 11.4 billion per second. For the Pi 5 the tutorial reports about 41 frames per second. Remove the 3.3 ms that the Pi 4 spends outside the model, and the estimate is 14.3 billion per second.

Treat these as first estimates and measure on your own robot. The software can change the answer by a large factor. Ultralytics reports a 2.4-million-parameter detector (YOLO26n) at 640 pixels on a Pi 5 in 32-bit arithmetic: 299 ms with PyTorch, 126 ms with ONNX and 67 ms with NCNN. The same network and the same computer give a factor of 4.5.

Memory and arithmetic differ

The table in the figure shows a second difference. Memory follows the number of weights. Time follows the number of multiply-adds. A convolutional network reuses a weight at all positions of the picture, so the digit reader does 32 multiply-adds per weight (117,912 for its 3,730 parameters), MobileNetV2 86 and ResNet-18 155. A language model uses a weight about once per token. The first group is usually limited by arithmetic and the second by how fast the memory can deliver the weights. The calculator counts arithmetic only. For GPT-2 and the 70-billion-parameter model its frames per second are therefore likely to be too high.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If your measured time is far from the calculator's, check three things. Is the program using all the cores of the computer? Did you time a warm run, not the first one? Does the time include copying the picture, which the model does not? Then compare the multiply-adds per second you measured with the speed you assumed.

Fewer bits per weight

Guess first. The digit reader of the CNN chapter is a small convolutional network that reads handwritten digits. It stores 3,702 weights as 32-bit numbers and reads 98.89% of the 10,000 test digits correctly. Round only the weights to 256 levels, which is 8 bits. How many of the 10,000 digits change their answer: none, about 6, about 600, or about 6,000?

Quantisation stores a weight with fewer bits by rounding it to the nearest of 2b evenly spaced levels, where b is the number of bits. The levels run from the smallest to the largest weight of a layer, and their spacing, the step, is the scale s. A rounding error, a weight minus its rounded value, is at most half a step, s/2. Layers have their own scales, and the 28 biases (added constants, 3,730 numbers in all with the weights) stay in 32 bits. In this example rounding to 8 bits cuts the memory of the weights by about four, because 8 is a quarter of 32, and changes the answer for 6 of the 10,000 test digits. At 3 and 2 bits the accuracy falls steeply.

  1. In the error plot of the dense layer (the last layer, with 3,000 weights), no rounding error at 8 bits exceeds 0.0048, half a step. The boxes show 6 changed answers and an accuracy of 98.87%.
  2. Choose 4 bits: the coral lines in the weights plot mark the allowed values, 184 digits change and the accuracy is 97.67%. Choose 2 bits: 7,910 digits change and the accuracy is 20.9%.
0memory for the weights (biases kept in 32 bits)
0accuracy on the 400 digits in your browser
0accuracy on all 10,000 test digits, measured offline
0digits that change their answer

At 8 bits the digit reader has an accuracy of 98.87% on the 10,000 test digits and 6 answers change; at 4 bits it has 97.67%, at 3 bits 92.16% and at 2 bits 20.9%.

How it works

Take the dense layer at 8 bits. Its smallest weight is wmin = −1.4644 and its largest is wmax = 0.9763, and 256 levels have 255 gaps, so s = (wmax − wmin)/(28 − 1) = 2.4407/255 = 0.009571. The zero point, the code that means 0.0, is z = round(−wmin/s) = 153. The first weight, w = −0.4328, is stored as the code q = round(w/s) + z = round(−45.2) + 153 = 108. It is rebuilt as s(q − z) = −0.4307, which is 0.0021 away, under half a step, 0.0048.

−0.4328weight w÷0.009571step s+153zero point z≈108stored code q→−0.4307s(q − z)→0.0021error, at most 0.0048

Removing one bit halves the number of levels, so s about doubles, and so does the largest error. At 8 bits the largest error is small next to the median absolute dense weight, 0.13. At 2 bits the step is 0.81, so the 2,748 of 3,000 dense weights with an absolute value under 0.41 are rounded to the level of zero.

Common belief. A bit removed always costs the same share of accuracy.

Why it fails. In this network the rounding error about halves with an added bit, yet the accuracy stays within 0.1 points of 98.89% down to 5 bits. It then falls to 92.16% at 3 bits.

Better account. Measure the accuracy at several widths on data like the robot's, and pick the smallest width that changes no important answer, with a margin.

Quick quiz

A layer has weights from −2 to 6. What is the step at 8 bits, and the largest rounding error?

\(s = 8/255 = 0.0314\). The largest error is \(s/2 = 0.0157\).

Why does the digit reader lose almost no accuracy at 8 bits and most of it at 2?

A likely reason, from the dense layer (the figure rounds all three layers, so this is not tested): at 8 bits the largest error, 0.0048, is small next to a typical weight, whose median absolute value is 0.13. At 2 bits the step is 0.81, so 2,748 of the 3,000 dense weights are rounded to the level of zero and lose their values.

Go deeper plots, why 8 bits works, symbols, Python about 5 min

What the plots show

The left plot shows a layer's weights. The coral lines, drawn when there are 32 levels or fewer, are the only values a quantised weight can take. At 8 bits there are 256 levels, so close together that they cannot be drawn. The right plot shows the rounding errors, weight minus stored value. At 8 bits they are spread about evenly between minus half a step and plus half a step. At 2 bits they are not, because most weights are rounded to zero and their errors are the weights themselves. When you remove a bit the step about doubles. The mean absolute error of all the weights is 0.0023 at 8 bits and 0.040 at 4 bits. That is 17 times larger, close to the 16 times that four doublings of the step give.

Why 8 bits works for this network

The weights of the dense layer run from −1.46 to 0.98, and the 8-bit step is 0.0096. The median absolute value of a dense weight is 0.13, and the error is at most half a step, 0.005, which is 4% of that. An output of the network sums 300 weights times activations, and rounding errors with both signs partly cancel in such a sum, a likely reason why the effect on the output is small. We measured the effect on the 400 digits in your browser: with 8-bit weights no output changes by more than 0.41, the 32-bit network's top answer leads the runner-up by a median of 8.9, and 1 of the 400 digits changes its answer. Over the 10,000 test digits, 6 flip. At 3 bits the step is 0.35, about 2.7 times the median weight, and 1,866 of the 3,000 dense weights are rounded to the level of zero. At 2 bits there are four levels, and 2,748 of the 3,000 are.

Rounding the activations too

The dotted line shows what happens when the activations, the numbers flowing between layers, are rounded to the same number of bits too. The ranges of the activations were taken from 500 training digits, as the LiteRT documentation advises (it asks for 100 to 500 samples). At 8 bits the result is 98.85%, within two digits of the weights-only result. This is one small network. The LiteRT page warns that there could be an accuracy loss, "particularly for smaller networks", and says to check it after conversion.

Small test sets

Compare the two accuracy readings at 8 bits. The 400 digits in your browser give 99.3%, above the 99.0% of the 32-bit network. The 10,000 test digits give 98.87% against 98.89%. Rounding does not train the network, and the rounded network gets 1 digit of the 400 right that the 32-bit network got wrong (397 against 396). One digit is 0.25 points of 400, so a small test set cannot show a change of a fraction of a point. The weights are those of the CNN chapter, trained on MNIST. The 10,000 test digits were run offline, and the 400 digits in your browser are the first 400 of them.

Symbols

0weight w÷0step s+0zero point z≈0stored code q→0s × (q − z)→0error, at most 0 here

\[ s = \frac{w_{\max} - w_{\min}}{2^{b} - 1} \qquad z = \operatorname{round}\!\left(\frac{-w_{\min}}{s}\right) \]

\[ q = \operatorname{clip}\!\left(\operatorname{round}\!\left(\frac{w}{s}\right) + z,\ 0,\ 2^{b}-1\right) \qquad \hat{w} = s\,(q - z) \qquad |w - \hat{w}| \le \frac{s}{2} \]

  • \(w\) is a weight and \(w_{\min}\), \(w_{\max}\) the smallest and largest weight of its layer. \(b\) is the bits per weight, so there are \(2^b\) codes, from 0 to \(2^b-1\).
  • \(s\) is the scale (the step between levels) and \(z\) the zero point. \(q\) is the integer that is stored. \(\hat w\) is the value the network uses when it computes; the program rebuilds it from \(q\).
  • The rounding step of the formula is why the error is at most \(s/2\), for any weight inside the range. The relation \(\hat w = s(q - z)\) is the one in the LiteRT quantisation specification and in Jacob and colleagues (2018). Hardware often fixes \(z = 0\) for weights (symmetric quantisation) and uses a scale per output channel. This page uses one scale and one zero point per layer, which is the simplest case.

Storage and arithmetic

A dense weight needs one byte instead of four. A network that runs with integers multiplies them and applies the scale once at the end of a sum. That is one reason 8-bit arithmetic can be fast on a chip with integer instructions.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. After quantising, run the 32-bit and the quantised model on the same inputs and count the answers that differ, as the "digits that change their answer" box does. Accuracy can stay the same while some digits swap in and out. Then look at the classes that matter most. A model can keep its average and lose the rare class (A4) or the murky-water frames (C3). If one outlier weight sets a layer's range, the step is large for all the others; a scale per output channel limits this to one channel.

In Python

import numpy as np

def quantise(w, bits):
    s = (w.max() - w.min()) / (2 ** bits - 1)     # scale: the step between levels
    z = int(round(-w.min() / s))                  # zero point: the code that means 0.0
    q = np.clip(np.round(w / s) + z, 0, 2 ** bits - 1).astype(int)
    return q, s, z

def dequantise(q, s, z):
    return s * (q - z)

w = np.array([-0.43, 0.12, 0.88, -1.46, 0.00])    # five made-up weights
for bits in (8, 4):
    q, s, z = quantise(w, bits)
    err = np.abs(w - dequantise(q, s, z))
    print(f"{bits} bits: step {s:.4f}, zero point {z}, codes {q.tolist()}, largest error {err.max():.4f}")
8 bits: step 0.0092, zero point 159, codes [112, 172, 255, 0, 159], largest error 0.0013
4 bits: step 0.1560, zero point 9, codes [6, 10, 15, 0, 9], largest error 0.0560

The ladder of model sizes

Guess first. A language model with 70 billion weights stores a weight in 2 bytes (16 bits). How much memory do the weights need: about 14 GB, about 140 GB, or about 1,400 GB?

This chapter covers two ways to make a model smaller. Its weights can be stored in fewer bits (a lower precision), or a network can be chosen that is designed to need fewer weights, such as MobileNetV2. The memory for the weights is the number of weights times the bytes per weight. From the digit reader to a 70-billion-parameter model the number of weights grows by a factor of about 19 million. Going from 32 bits to 8 shrinks the memory by a factor of 4, because a weight then takes 1 byte instead of 4.

  1. Find ResNet-18 in the table: 46.8 MB at 32 bits and 11.7 MB at 8 bits, a quarter of that.
  2. In the row of the 70-billion-parameter model no entry is green. Even at 4 bits it needs 35 GB, above the dashed 4, 8 and 16 GB lines.

Green figures fit in 4 GB, the memory of the Pi 4 above. Weights only: the picture, the activations, the program and (for language models) the KV cache take more.

ResNet-18 needs 46.8 MB at 32 bits and 11.7 MB at 8 bits, and the 70-billion-parameter model needs 280 GB at 32 bits and 35 GB even at 4 bits, more than the 16 GB of the largest Raspberry Pi 5.

How it works

Take ResNet-18, which has 11,689,512 weights. A weight takes 4, 2, 1 or 0.5 bytes at 32, 16, 8 or 4 bits. The memory is therefore 11,689,512 times that number of bytes. The same sum answers the guess: 70 × 109 weights × 2 bytes = 140 GB.

11,689,512ResNet-18 weights×4, 2, 1, 0.5bytes per weight at 32, 16, 8 and 4 bits=46.8, 23.4, 11.7, 5.8MB

The second way is a smaller network. MobileNetV2 has 3.5 million weights and 301 million multiply-adds, and ResNet-18 has 11.7 million and 1,814 million, which is 3.3 times the memory and 6 times the arithmetic. Fewer bits shrink the memory but not always the time. A processor with no 4-bit multiply may unpack 4-bit weights to 8 bits first, so the calculator of the second section gives 4 bits the speed of 8.

Common belief. A model that fits in memory will run well on the robot.

Why it fails. Fitting is the first of several tests. The robot also needs the model to meet the time budget of the loop and to keep its accuracy at the lower precision. The rest of the program needs memory too: the activations (numbers passed between layers), the program and, for a language model, the KV cache, which grows with the text.

Better account. Run three checks in order: memory, time per frame, accuracy on the robot's own pictures. Test the cheapest first.

Quick quiz

GPT-2 small has 124,439,808 weights. How much memory in 16 bits, and does it fit in 1 GB?

\(124{{,}}439{{,}}808\times 2 = 248.9\) MB, about a quarter of 1 GB. The weights fit. The activations, the program and the KV cache need space too.

Why is a 4-bit model smaller than an 8-bit one, and why might it not be faster on a Pi?

A weight takes half the bytes, so the memory halves. A processor with no 4-bit multiply may have to unpack the weights to 8 bits before the arithmetic. Then the number of multiply-adds and their speed stay the same.

Go deeper bars, smaller networks, memory beyond the weights about 2 min

The bars

The ladder of the title is the models of this primer in order of weights: the digit reader, MobileNetV2, ResNet-18, GPT-2 small and a large language model. The 70 billion is the size of the largest Llama 2 model (Touvron and others, 2023). The bars are the memory for the weights. A model has four bars, one per precision. The dashed lines are the memory of a small computer. The digit reader needs 15 KB. MobileNetV2 and ResNet-18 need tens of MB in 32 bits, which any Pi can store easily. GPT-2 small needs 498 MB at 32 bits and 62 MB at 4 bits, so it fits in 4 GB at all four precisions. The large model does not fit anywhere on the page. It needs a much larger computer, or a robot that sends its pictures to a computer on shore.

The second way to a smaller model

Sandler and colleagues (2018) built MobileNetV2 for mobile devices, where this trade matters. Which of the two networks finds sharks better depends on the data, and this chapter does not compare them. Test both networks on murky-water frames before you choose (C3). Other ways to shrink a model exist, such as removing weights or training a small model to copy a large one, and this chapter does not cover them.

The weights are not the whole memory

The weights are not the whole memory. A running network also needs memory for its activations, the feature maps between layers, and the program that runs it. A language model also keeps a KV cache that grows with the text: for GPT-2 small, 37.7 MB at 1,024 tokens in 16 bits (D5). Leave headroom and measure the memory of the running process.

Exercises

Theory

  1. theory GPT-2 small has 124,439,808 weights. Work out the memory of its weights at 32, 16, 8 and 4 bits. Which of these fit in a computer with 1 GB, and what else must fit?

  2. theory A network does 900 million multiply-adds per frame. A computer reaches 9 billion per second with 8-bit weights, and 32-bit arithmetic is 2.5 times slower. Find the frames per second at 8 and at 32 bits. The robot needs 8 frames per second. Which precision meets the need?

  3. theory A layer has weights between −0.8 and 1.2 and is stored in 4 bits. Find the scale \(s\) and the zero point \(z\). Quantise the weight 0.30, rebuild it, and state the largest error any weight in this range can have.

    Hint

    There are \(2^4 - 1 = 15\) steps between the smallest and the largest weight.

  4. theory A shark crosses at 0.8 m/s, 2 m from the camera. The camera may be at most 4 degrees behind. Using \(\omega = v/d\), find the longest allowed \(L + T\). A loop has \(L = 150\) ms. What is the largest update period \(T\) it can have?

Practice

  1. practice Write quantise and dequantise in NumPy as in the chapter. For a random normal array of 10,000 numbers, find the mean absolute error for 2 to 10 bits. Check that it roughly halves with an added bit and that no error exceeds \(s/2\).

  2. practice Load data/quant.json from this chapter and quantise fc_w (3,000 weights) to 8, 6 and 4 bits. For the three widths, count how many weights fall in the same level as zero (the code \(z\)). What does the count say about 4 bits?

  3. practice With PyTorch, time one forward pass of torchvision.models.resnet18() and mobilenet_v2() on a 1 by 3 by 224 by 224 input, using one thread and a warm-up. Divide the multiply-adds (1.814 and 0.301 billion) by the times. How does your computer's speed compare with the Pi's 11.4 billion per second at 8 bits?

Think deeper

  1. open SharkCam must detect sharks at 5 frames per second on a Pi with 4 GB, for two hours on a battery. Which model and which precision would you try first? What would you measure after quantising to be sure the rare Ganges shark is still found, and how would you test in murky water?

    Hint

    The average accuracy can stay the same while a rare class disappears. Think of recall for one class, and of A4's lazy model.

  2. open The robot could run the model on its own small computer, or send the pictures to a computer on shore. Suppose the link is slow and sometimes drops. List what the two designs gain and lose in latency, memory, battery and what happens when the link fails.

  3. open The calculator ignores the battery. How would you find out how much energy one frame costs, and how would that change your choice between MobileNetV2 and ResNet-18?

Come back later

Try after two days. In C2 the digit reader had 3,730 numbers and a plain network on the same task had 101,770. Which of the two sums of this chapter does that change, memory or time, and which one depends on weight sharing?

Both change, in different ways. Memory follows the number of weights, so the plain network needs 27 times more. The time follows the multiply-adds. In a CNN a shared weight is used at all positions, so the multiply-adds per weight are large (32 for the digit reader). See C2.

Try after a week. A4 says a model that never flags a Ganges shark is 99.5% accurate. Why does that matter when you quantise the SharkCam model?

Rounding the weights can change a few answers. If they are the rare ones, overall accuracy hardly moves and the model stops finding the rare shark. So check recall for the rare class before and after, as well as accuracy (A4).

Try after a week. D5 gave the KV cache size as 2 × layers × tokens × width × bytes. Which bit width would you use to shrink it on a robot, and what would you check?

The cache is numbers too, so fewer bits per number shrink it in the same way, with the same trade: less memory, more rounding. Check the model's answers on long inputs with the smaller cache against the full one (D5).

Sources and further reading

  1. Jacob, B., Kligys, S., Chen, B., Zhu, M., Tang, M., Howard, A., Adam, H. and Kalenichenko, D. (2018). Quantization and training of neural networks for efficient integer-arithmetic-only inference. CVPR 2018. arXiv:1712.05877. The scale and zero point scheme used here.
  2. Google (LiteRT documentation). 8-bit quantization specification: the value is (int8 value − zero point) × scale, with weights per axis or per tensor and zero point 0. developers.google.com/edge/litert/models/quantization_spec.
  3. Google (LiteRT documentation). Post-training quantization: dynamic range and full integer quantization, a representative dataset of about 100 to 500 samples, and the warning about accuracy loss in smaller networks. developers.google.com/edge/litert/performance/post_training_quantization.
  4. PyTorch tutorials. Running MobileNetV2 on a Raspberry Pi 4 and 5. MobileNetV2 quantised to 8 bits, on a Pi 4 with 4 GB: 26.4 ms in the model, 29.7 ms per frame and about 3.5 ms to read and resize the picture; about 41 frames per second on a Pi 5. docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/intermediate/realtime_rpi.html.
  5. Ultralytics documentation. Raspberry Pi guide: benchmarks of YOLO26n at 640 pixels in 32-bit on a Pi 5 (PyTorch 299 ms, ONNX 126 ms, NCNN 67 ms), docs.ultralytics.com/guides/raspberry-pi/. YOLO26 models: 2.4 million parameters for the n size, docs.ultralytics.com/models/yolo26/.
  6. Raspberry Pi Ltd. Raspberry Pi 5: a 2.4 GHz quad-core Arm Cortex-A76 and 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 GB of memory. raspberrypi.com/products/raspberry-pi-5/. Raspberry Pi 4 Model B: a 1.8 GHz quad-core Arm Cortex-A72, sold with 1 to 8 GB. raspberrypi.com/products/raspberry-pi-4-model-b/.
  7. PyTorch documentation. Quantization. docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/quantization.html. The page now points new work to the torchao library; the Raspberry Pi tutorial above uses the quantised MobileNetV2 of torchvision.
  8. He, K., Zhang, X., Ren, S. and Sun, J. (2015). Deep residual learning for image recognition. arXiv:1512.03385 (CVPR 2016). The architecture of ResNet-18; the counts here are from the torchvision definition.
  9. Sandler, M., Howard, A., Zhu, M., Zhmoginov, A. and Chen, L.-C. (2018). MobileNetV2: inverted residuals and linear bottlenecks. CVPR, 4510–4520.
  10. Touvron, H. and others (2023). Llama 2: open foundation and fine-tuned chat models. arXiv:2307.09288. Models from 7 to 70 billion parameters.
  11. The digits and the digit reader are those of C2 (MNIST, with the citation given there). The sizes of GPT-2 and its KV cache come from D5.
